papers.title_in_file: Balanced k-Means Clustering on an Adiabatic Quantum Computer
papers.version_note: arXiv:2008.04419v1 [cs.LG] 10 Aug 2020. The text layer is the paper once; the reference list sits between the Conclusion and the last lines of the Conclusion because of the page layout.
papers.what_it_is: A QUBO formulation of balanced k-means clustering, run on a D-Wave 2000Q for problems of up to 64 binary variables and compared with scikit-learn k-means and a classical balanced k-means algorithm on synthetic data and Iris subsets.

existing.value: The authors state that, owing to qubit limits of the hardware, problems that need more than 64 binary variables are impossible on the D-Wave 2000Q, and the entire Iris data set could not be clustered.
quotes: problems that require more than 64 binary variables (N k > 64) are impossible on the D-Wave 2000Q
Unfortunately, due to qubit limitations on modern hardware, it is impossible to perform quantum balanced k-means clustering on the entire data set.
existing.certainty_reason: Section IV-B6 and Section IV-C state the limit of the hardware used.

existing.note: The sentence is from the data-point scalability study (k = 4, d = 2). The quantum run times in that study are not measured on the hardware: embedding time and annealing time are estimated (embedding by an extrapolated formula, annealing as the mean of the small experiments); only formulation and postprocessing are measured. The same direction is reported for the cluster-count and feature-count studies.
existing.value: The authors report that, in the data-point scalability study (k = 4 classes, d = 2 features), the quantum approach performed slower than both classical algorithms in each case, that the quantum run time was dominated by the embedding time, and that embedding and annealing times for these problem sizes were estimated rather than measured on the hardware.
quotes: In each case, the quantum approach performed slower than both classical algorithms. However, the quantum run time was dominated by the embedding time.
Each data set contained k = 4 classes, and each data point had d = 2 features.
We estimate the time required to embed the problem (te) as well as annealing time (ta).
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, partly based on estimated times.
existing.reader_inference: The slower-in-every-case result is partly an artifact of an extrapolated embedding time added to a measured formulation time; it is not a wall-clock run on hardware at those sizes (N k above 64 cannot run).

existing.note: The Conclusion states similar accuracy, but the results sections limit it: the classical balanced k-means algorithm had the best performance for most synthetic experiments, the classical algorithms did better at k = 2, and quantum performance degrades as problem size grows. Only small problems (up to 64 binary variables) were run.
existing.value: The authors state that they demonstrated that their quantum approach partitions data with similar accuracy to the classical approaches, even when running on imperfect hardware; their results sections also report that the classical balanced k-means algorithm had the best performance for most synthetic experiments, that the classical algorithms performed better for k = 2 on Iris subsets, and that the performance of the quantum algorithm degrades as problem size increases.

assertions.value: The authors state that, provided N is divisible by k and the penalty constants alpha and beta are large enough to ensure all constraints are upheld, Problem 16 and Problem 4 share the same global solution.

assertions.certainty_reason: Section III derives the penalty form step by step and states the condition under which the QUBO and the balanced k-means problem share the global solution.
assertions.reader_inference: An informal derivation, not a numbered theorem; the paper gives no value of alpha and beta that is proved sufficient (the chosen values in Section III-A are described as the best performing in practice).

assertions.value: The authors state that the total number of variables in Equation 16 is O(N k), which translates to a quadratic qubit footprint of O(N 2k2) (printed flat; order N squared times k squared) using an efficient embedding algorithm such as the one in reference 30.
quotes: Thus, the total number of variables in Equation 16 is O(N k).
This translates to a quadratic qubit footprint of O(N 2k2) using an efﬁcient embedding algorithm such as [30].
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling statement tied to a cited embedding algorithm; the paper gives no derivation of the qubit footprint.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I (nine settings, up to 64 variables) shows qubit counts several times the variable count in every setting, which is consistent with a superlinear footprint.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table I, for nine (N, k) settings, the number of binary variables and the average number of qubits used by the quantum approach; the largest settings use 64 binary variables.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from Equation 19, the worst case time complexity of forming the QUBO is O(N 2kd) (printed flat; order N squared times k times d) and that the total time complexity of the quantum algorithm is O(N 2kd); provided kd < N this is better than the O(N 3) of the best classical balanced k-means algorithm but worse than the O(N kd) of the Scikit-learn generic k-means.
quotes: From Equation 19, the worst case time complexity is O(N 2kd)
Therefore, the total time complexity of the quantum algorithm is O(N 2kd).
Provided kd < N , this time complexity is better than the time complexity of the best classical balanced k-means clustering algorithm (O(N 3)).
However, it is worse than the Scikit-learn implementation of generic k-means clustering (O(N kd)).
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal complexity count resting on the constant-time annealing assumption; the paper does not state it as a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: The total excludes embedding time, which the paper's own experiments show dominates and which grows quadratically with the number of binary variables N k (so order N squared k squared, above N squared k d whenever k exceeds d).

assertions.value: The authors state that, for practical purposes, solving the QUBO problem through quantum annealing can be done in constant time, and that annealing is performed in constant time; for larger problems they therefore assume the annealing time equals the average annealing time of the small clustering experiments.

Therefore, we assume that the annealing time for larger problems (ta) is equal to the average annealing time for the small clustering experiments discussed in Section IV-B5.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sections IV-A and IV-B6 state the assumption that the scaling analysis and the time estimates are built on.
assertions.reader_inference: The constant-time assumption is an input to every quantum-versus-classical scaling comparison in the paper; the paper gives no evidence for it at sizes above those run.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in practice, they achieved the best performance with alpha scaled from max(D) and beta equal to max(D), where max(D) is the maximum element in D, and that this scaling rests on the assumption that the training data set has well defined clusters.

β = max(D)

Assuming the training data set has well deﬁned clusters, the maximum element of D is much larger than the average squared distance between two points in a given cluster.

assertions.reader_inference: The constants were tuned for performance in practice, not derived; the equivalence condition (large enough penalties) is separate from these values.

assertions.value: The authors state that by multiplying F by a smaller factor than G they guarantee that row constraints are more strictly enforced than column constraints, which permits small violations of the equal-size cluster constraint when N is not divisible by k.
quotes: By multiplying F by a smaller factor than G, we also guarantee that row constraints are more strictly enforced than column constraints.
This is desirable since we would like to permit small violations of the equal-size cluster constraint when N is not divisible by k.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III-A states a design choice of the formulation.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Guarantee' refers to the relative size of the penalty weights, not to the annealer's output, which the next paragraph says can violate constraints.

assertions.value: The authors state that, in practice, the quantum annealing process is not perfect and instances occur in which a point is assigned to multiple clusters or to no cluster; a point assigned to multiple clusters is taken to belong to the cluster with the smaller index, and a point assigned to no cluster is taken to belong to the first cluster.
quotes: In practice the quantum annealing process is not perfect, and instances occur in which a point is assigned to multiple clusters or not assigned to any cluster at all.
If quantum annealing assigns a point to multiple clusters, we consider the point to belong to the cluster with the smaller index.
If quantum annealing does not assign a point to any cluster, we consider the point to belong to the ﬁrst cluster.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III-A states the repair rules used on annealer output and the limit of the annealer.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not report how often constraint violations occurred; ARI is computed after these arbitrary repairs.

assertions.value: The authors state that adiabatic quantum computers are able to find the global minimum of the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem.
quotes: Adiabatic quantum computers are able to ﬁnd the global minimum of the quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The Introduction says the D-Wave 2000Q 'approximately solves' QUBO, and Section III-A says annealing 'is not perfect'; the global-minimum wording is a premise of the paper's global-solution argument, not a result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the D-Wave 2000Q adiabatic quantum computer approximately solves the NP-complete quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem efficiently, and that modern quantum computers are too small and error-prone to effectively solve large problems.

The Scikit-learn implementation of Lloyd’s algorithm bounds the number of iterations by a constant, effectively reducing the time complexity to O(N kd) [18].

assertions.value: The authors state that, while many quantum clustering algorithms have been proposed, none target the exact solution to the k-means or balanced k-means clustering model, and that their QUBO formulation is identical to the balanced k-means training problem.
quotes: While many quantum clustering algorithms have been proposed, none target the exact solution to the k-means or balanced k-means clustering model.
We propose a QUBO formulation that is identical to the balanced k-means training problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's novelty claim without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Identical' holds only under the conditions in the equivalence assertion (N divisible by k, large enough penalties); the paper's own Section III-A says N not divisible by k is permitted with small violations.

assertions.value: The authors report that the quantum approach was tested on the D-Wave 2000Q and compared with the Scikit-learn implementation of classical k-means and with their own implementation of the classical balanced k-means algorithm, using two metrics, adjusted rand index and total computing time; Scikit-learn k-means searches for a solution to Problem 2, while the balanced algorithm and the quantum approach search for Problem 4.
quotes: Our quantum approach was tested on the D-Wave 2000Q adiabatic quantum computer.
Note that the Scikit-learn implementation of k-means searches for a solution to Problem 2, while the classical balanced k-means algorithm and our quantum approach search for a solution to Problem 4.
We use two performance metrics to compare the three algorithms: (i) adjusted rand index and (ii) total computing time.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV-B1 states the comparison set-up.
assertions.reader_inference: The generic-k-means baseline solves a different problem from the other two; the authors argue the solutions should be very similar for their data sets, which they do not show.

assertions.value: The authors state that total computing time in the quantum approach is composed of the time to convert the problem into a QUBO problem, the time to embed the QUBO problem on the hardware, the annealing time, and the postprocessing time.

assertions.value: The authors state that they show their quantum approach better targets the global solution of the training problem, while achieving better theoretic scalability on large datasets, and that they test it on a number of small problems and observe clustering performance similar to the best classical algorithms.
quotes: We show that our quantum approach better targets the global solution of the training problem, while achieving better theoretic scalability on large datasets.
We test our quantum approach on a number of small problems, and observe clustering performance similar to the best classical algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's summary claim; the support is the penalty-equivalence argument and the complexity count, each with stated caveats.
assertions.reader_inference: 'Better targets the global solution' depends on the annealer finding the global minimum (see the global-minimum premise), which the paper's own Section III-A says does not always happen. The 'better theoretic scalability' compares O(N 2kd) with O(N 3) and omits embedding.

assertions.value: The authors state in the Conclusion that they show their approach targets the global solution of the training problem better than its classical alternatives and scales favorably on large data sets compared with current classical balanced k-means algorithms, and that they expect their approach to become a viable alternative to existing classical balanced clustering algorithms as quantum hardware continues to improve in both fidelity and scale.
quotes: We analyze our approach theoretically, showing that it targets the global solution of the training problem better than its classical alternatives.
We also show that our approach scales favorably on large data sets when compared to current classical balanced k-means algorithms.
As quantum hardware continues to improve in both ﬁdelity and scale, we expect our approach to become a viable alternative to existing classical balanced clustering algorithms.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion and projection without evidence at the sizes claimed.
assertions.reader_inference: In every measured scaling study the quantum approach was slower than both classical algorithms; the 'favorable scaling' rests on the O(N 2kd) count and on extrapolated embedding and annealing times.

assertions.value: The authors state as future work that they hope to generalize their QUBO formulation to satisfy the generic k-means clustering training problem (Problem 2), to formulate quantum algorithms for similar models such as k-medoids or fuzzy C-means clustering, and to investigate quantum approaches to clustering larger datasets within the qubit constraints of modern hardware.
